title: Elucidating the Design Space of Regression-based Diffusion Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: Elucidating the Design Space of Regression-based Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract A nascent family of methods that forgoes the policy gradient and reweights a supervised regression instead has garnered momentum in reinforcement learning for diffusion and flow models. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , FlowAWR ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , and RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) are representative regimes with contrasting motivations. It is yet opaque what, if anything, they share. We substantiate that each is the solution of one divergence-constrained reward-maximization problem, and they are differentiated only by the convex generator that defines the constraint. Under the unified modeling framework, we unravel the relaxations that prior art made during building the advantage-embedded regression target: approximating the KKT condition and posterior normalizer for the linear and exponential tilt shapes DiffusionNFT and FlowAWR respectively, while preserving the exact sparsemax projection onto the probability simplex for linear tilt leads to another superior model type in this work. Beyond the theoretical underpinnings, we further empirically investigate the design space and shed light on the training recipe for regression-style diffusion RL. Retaining the merits discovered during our exploration gives rise to DiffusionRFT, our paradigm that converges faster, trains more stably, and attains the top performance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Post-training with an external reward plays a pivotal role in endowing a diffusion model with human-preference behaviors that pre-training dictates only weakly, such as prompt adherence and text rendering. Reinforcement learning serves as a cornerstone of this utility. The trailblazers in this field are the policy gradient ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ) and direct reward backpropagation ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2024 ) scheme. Nevertheless, they are both cumbersome, in that a long denoising trajectory is indispensable and exhibits high variance. Moreover, the training objective diverges from the simple Mean-Squared Error (MSE) loss prevalent in pre-training, that is believed to simplify the generative distribution modeling to supervised learning, especially at scale. Recently, a growing body of forward-process policy optimization ushers in a new wave of diffusion RL, including DiffusionNFT, FlowAWR and RAM, which reserve the regular diffusion loss and inject a reward into the regression target, so that a policy update is again a least-square fit on noised samples. These algorithms are grounded in divergent perspectives, ranging from CFG-style contrastive rectification Chen et al. (2025) to stochastic optimal control ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) . Worse still, they are separately presented as standalone and integrated systems. The missing piece is a principled account of their subtle interweaving, and which design decisions drive the performance. To bridge this gap, we uncover that one optimization step underlying these RL algorithms converges to a common driving force: maximize reward on a frozen rollout buffer under a divergence penalty. The divergence penalty translates the primary algorithmic choice into a single convex generator f f (equation 2 ). The reverse-KL generator yields the exponential tilt, whose group estimator coincides with the FlowAWR objective, while the Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} generator yields a linear tilt, that DiffusionNFT already applies by standardizing the reward within a prompt group and dividing by a heuristic constant, but without such a derivation. As stated above, permitting the realization of the unified optimization objective demands an additional approximation, estimating a posterior normalizer by its endpoint counterpart. We demonstrate it preserves the direction of every step exactly while rescaling its length by a factor with unit mean and variance bounded by the second moment of the advantage. The Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} case turns out to be the more promising one, to which most of our research endeavor is devoted. Its exact constrained optimum is a Euclidean projection onto the probability simplex, that is the sparsemax weight, whereas the linear advantage heuristically adopted by DiffusionNFT keeps only the interior branch of the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions and silently drops the constraint that relative densities stay non-negative. We articulate the condition under which the dense form is exact, observe that it is violated by the dense linear tilt on most training steps, and the training collapses afterwards. Retaining the projection repairs the collapse and achieves higher rewards. We term our resulting method Diffusion Regression Fine-tuning , or DiffusionRFT, a notably more stable and efficient point in this design space. Beyond the scope of our derivation lie the empirical design choices. The remainder is cast into four axes: the regression variable, the reward shaping and its baseline, the anchor from which the target is displaced, and the law governing the renoising timestep, and we adjust each in isolation. The regression variable lays the groundwork for subsequent algorithmic axes. Empirical results advocate the sparsemax tilt in line with our exact derivation. Meanwhile, an analytically variance-minimizing baseline further facilitates performance stabilization and enhancement across all tilts. A frozen anchor, though supported by RAM, admits no safe operating point, regardless of the update magnitude. Decoupling the renoising timestep from the generating trajectory, which might be assumed to enrich the experience buffer, instead steers the loss toward noise levels the sampler never visits.

sections.heading: 3 From a Heuristic Linear Tilt to the Exact Simplex Projection
sections.text: DiffusionNFT contrasts two implicit branches of the same model rather than forming a density ratio, so its update needs no likelihood ELBO ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ) . For the same reason, it never states which divergence it controls. This section recovers that information and places the family inside § 2.1 . We find that a single DiffusionNFT update is a least-square regression onto a target of the advantage-weighted form, and that the reward enters that target linearly rather than exponentially . § 3.1 puts the update in regression form and records the general statement that any endpoint reweighting induces such a target; § 3.2 derives the reverse-KL counterpart, the exponential tilt, which coincides with the concurrently proposed FlowAWR objective; § 3.3 identifies that a linear tilt is exactly what the Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} penalty produces, but that its constrained optimum is a sparsemax projection of which the dense linear form is only the interior branch.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experiment settings
sections.text: For a fair comparison and reproducibility, we follow DiffusionNFT’s codebase to adapt other follow-up variants. The training and evaluation dataset is GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) , that measures compositional spatial reasoning in text-to-image tasks. All experiments are conducted with the Stable Diffusion 3.5-Medium backbone ( Esser et al., 2024 ) at a 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution. Other experimental details and additional results on Pickscore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) are provided in appendix G .

sections.heading: loss function
sections.text: We start from equation 15 , a widely acknowledged exponential tilt, to launch our exploration. We find that the 𝒗 {\bm{v}} -prediction described in prior literature ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) converges slowly in training, agreeing with the gap between theoretical justification and empirical implementation, as mentioned by Kveton et al. (2026) . Consequently, we adopt 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -prediction to expedite training hereafter, in light of a sharp gap displayed in figure 2 (a). Furthermore, certain subtle implementation details decide training dynamics. Particularly, the loss scaling factor and self-normalization accelerate training convergence. These points of interest are elaborated in another contemporary work in the context of diffusion distillation ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . The training dynamics in figure 2 show that the gap concerns the update direction, not magnitude. At a matched horizon the 𝒗 {\bm{v}} -prediction run carries the largest advantage and spends the largest movement budget, but gains the least reward, while its regression loss is an order of magnitude higher than 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -prediction. An empirical decomposition constrains several contributors, e.g. advantage scale, prediction units, and residual excess, only loosely, leaving room for the change in the irreducible floor alone to account for the observed loss ratio. In particular, the 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -space loss eschews the coefficient t − 2 t^{-2} with which the 𝒗 {\bm{v}} -space loss uplifts the endpoint’s irreducible inflation. Appendix H delves deeper into the rationale. The resulting + 0.34 +0.34 gain in the terminal training reward is pronounced, so we fix this loss geometry throughout rather than treating it as one more knob.

Replacing 𝒇 old {\bm{f}}_{\mathrm{old}} by 𝒇 ref {\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}} alone produces an anchor-lock phenomenon: the training reward of three frozen-anchor variants (with different tilt and regression space) rises to below 0.25 0.25 and stagnates, so the ceiling is a property of the anchor and not of one particular setup. The culprit of lock is limited displacement ‖ 𝒇 θ − 𝒇 anchor ‖ 2 \|{\bm{f}}_{\theta}-{\bm{f}}_{\text{anchor}}\|^{2} , not a starved signal. In figure 3 , the frozen-anchor runs carry larger advantages than the rolling-anchor one, yet they never leave the pretrained field, even though the local change is non-negligible from the outset. With the anchor fixed the target is 𝒇 ref + 𝒜 ​ δ {\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}}+\mathcal{A}\,\delta , so each update re-centers the policy to 𝒇 ref {\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}} and the attainable displacement is bounded by the advantage-weighted residual itself, whereas a rolling anchor 𝒇 old {\bm{f}}_{\mathrm{old}} tracks 𝒇 θ {\bm{f}}_{\theta} closely. sections.heading: experience buffer
sections.text: The training states 𝒙 t {\bm{x}}_{t} are renoised from the generated clean samples, where the renoising timesteps are tied to the backward denoising trajectory, which is reminiscent of the classic replay buffer in RL ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Differently, RAM decouples the forward renoising timestep schedule from the denoising trajectory: renoise timesteps are drawn from a uniform distribution and repeated K = 8 K=8 times, accumulating an 8 × 8\times experience buffer for one-step optimization. RAM’s sampling conflates two factors at once, the law of t t and the number of copies K K . Crossing the two achieves evaluation rewards of 0.972 0.972 & 0.975 0.975 for the trajectory-coupled law at K = 1 K=1 & K = 8 K=8 , against 0.964 0.964 & 0.953 0.953 for the uniform law, the last of these losing a further 0.086 0.086 before the budget ends (figure 4 ). Expanding sampling K K is therefore neutral and it is the law of t t that counts. The underlying cause is that decoupling alters the support of t t : the sampler-oriented distribution never visits t < 0.43 t<0.43 (figure 7 ), while t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] places 43 % 43\% of the loss evaluations there. It also clarifies why two variance-reduction remedies, stratified sampling and shared ( t , ϵ ) (t,\epsilon) sampling across copies ( Tang et al., 2026 ) , still fail, and why stratification, that enforces the uniform coverage, is even the more damaging of these two. Renoising along the generating trajectory only once ( K = 1 K=1 ) keeps the training states on the support the policy occupies, which is both cheaper and better conditioned, so we retain it by default. Appendix H incorporates more in-depth diagnostics.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Regression-based reinforcement learning for diffusion models admits a unified formulation with a free parameter. The convex generator in the divergence penalty determines the particular choice of this parameter: an exponential tilt for FlowAWR; a linear tilt whose exact solution, the sparsemax projection, leads to our proposed DiffusionRFT; DiffusionNFT heuristically adopts the dense linear form that lies in the interior branch of the latter. The empirical picture favors getting the tilt done right. Standing on its own, the projected linear tilt performs the best among them, and it is the only candidate that does not surrender its peak reward; a variance-minimizing baseline then stabilizes and improves all three tilts, and the two together approach the fastest convergence and highest reward. Besides the tilt choice, what bears emphasis includes 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -prediction with appropriate loss calibration, an online cumulative anchor point, and a backward-aligned forward renoising schedule.

sections.heading: A.1 Diffusion Generative Modeling
sections.text: Inspired by thermodynamics ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) in physics, the advent of diffusion models occurred one decade ago. In the following years, after briefly overshadowed by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) , improved empirical practice ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and a firmer theoretical footing ( Song et al., 2021b ) ignited the resurgence of diffusion generative modeling. The system is further scaled up with advanced architecture engineering ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , distribution coupling ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , network capacity reallocation ( Karras et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ; Kingma and Gao, 2023 ) , and higher-order solvers ( Song et al., 2021a ; Lu et al., 2022 ) . Embracing diffusion as the generative modeling backend, recent years have witnessed an unprecedented achievement across a variety of visual generative applications, such as text-to-image ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , video ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Team Seedance et al., 2026 ) , and 3D geometry ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Thanks to the pixel-level generative modeling, diffusion models permit a supervised learning MSE loss to be established and optimized stably (much more than GANs’ brittle minimax game). Nevertheless, a coin always has two sides: this training objective also falls short of straightforwardly modeling the sample-level human preference, such as visual aesthetics, physical plausibility, among others.

sections.heading: A.2 Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has gained tremendous traction in Large Language Models (LLMs), contributing to both alignment with human preference ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and incentivization of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . The transfer of RL in autoregressive modeling to diffusion models poses a challenge, as there is no well-defined tractable likelihood formulation in diffusion modeling. One paradigm converts the deterministic ODE solver into a stochastic SDE, in order to frame each transition as a step of a Markovian Decision Process (MDP) and supplies the exploration noise that policy-gradient estimators require ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Another strand sidesteps the likelihood calculation via directly back-propagating a differentiable reward through the sampler ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2024 ) . Instead, DiffusionNFT innovatively presents the first diffusion-native RL prototype, through the lens of implicit contrastive learning between positive and negative representation fields ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . However, the underlying insight of its reward-integrated regression target is not disclosed. Likewise, several recent works ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Xue et al., 2026 ; Kveton et al., 2026 ) also lie in the lineage of advantage-weighted regression ( Peng et al., 2019 ) , where a reward-tilted distribution is fitted by weighted least squares rather than followed by a gradient. Mindful of its design elegance and the built-in compatibility with diffusion loss, we first link the DiffusionNFT formulation to the classic constrained reward maximization problem, and then venture as far as possible into the design space.

sections.heading: Appendix G Implementation and experimental details
sections.text: Every run in § 4 adopts the following setup inherited from DiffusionNFT, although it may place our methods at a disadvantage.

sections.heading: Backbone and adapters.
sections.text: SD3.5-Medium at 512 2 512^{2} pix resolution, loaded in fp16 mixed precision. Only LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) adapters are trained, at rank r = 32 r=32 with scaling α = 64 \alpha=64 , while the backbone is frozen. This makes the frozen-anchor variants of § 4.2 inexpensive, since the pretrained field 𝒇 ref {\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}} is recovered by disabling the adapters, so no second copy of the weights is held in memory.

sections.heading: Prompt pool and evaluation set.
sections.text: Both splits are the GenEval metadata shipped with the DiffusionNFT codebase. The training pool holds 50,000 50{,}000 records spanning 33,199 33{,}199 distinct prompts and the evaluation split holds 2,212 2{,}212 records over the 553 553 distinct prompts of the GenEval benchmark, four records per prompt, and is evaluated in full at every evaluation round rather than subsampled.

sections.heading: Rollout and buffer.
sections.text: An epoch draws 48 48 prompts and samples each G = 24 G=24 times, for 1,152 1{,}152 images per epoch. The prompt count follows from the sampler rather than being set directly: with 8 8 devices, a per-device batch of 9 9 and G = 24 G=24 images per prompt, each batch covers 8 × 9 / 24 = 3 8\times 9/24=3 prompts, and an epoch runs 16 16 such batches. Sampling uses a T = 10 T=10 step first-order Euler solver on the flow-matching schedule with shift 3.0 3.0 , and is CFG-free ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . Each buffer is consumed by a single optimization iteration before the next rollout, so no endpoint is revisited and the frozen-buffer premise of § 2.1 holds. By default the loss is evaluated at the timesteps the rollout itself visited, which is the coupling that axis (iv) isolates. A fraction 90 % 90\% of the schedule is retained, which merely excludes the degenerated endpoint.

sections.heading: Optimization.
sections.text: AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) with β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} and weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} is utilized, at a constant learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} . The micro-batch size is 9 9 latents per device with 16 16 gradient-accumulation steps. Gradients are clipped to unit norm and an exponential moving average of the adapters is maintained. Both are kept fixed across all runs, so the gradient norms reported in § 4.2 are the pre-clipping values and remain comparable between configurations. The loss scale is s = 5.0 s=5.0 , which is also the s s entering η eff \eta_{\text{eff}} in equation 57 . For the exponential tilt, γ \gamma is set adaptively to the reward standard deviation pooled across the batch and floored at 0.01 0.01 , and no advantage clipping is applied unless an ablation asks for it. All runs use seed 42 42 for reproducibility.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Evaluation runs every 10 10 epochs with a 40 40 -step first-order solver, four times the rollout budget, so that a policy cannot appear to improve merely by adapting to a coarse sampler. No run is stopped early on a training episode. Each is trained until it either plateaus or collapses, within a maximum budget of 1,000 1{,}000 epochs, and the horizon shown in a figure is the horizon that was run.

sections.heading: Diagnosis metrics.
sections.text: We also fix three quantities that we record for every run and that turn out to explain most of what we observe in the incoming section. The first is the effective step size η eff = s ⋅ 𝔼 ​ | 𝒜 | , \eta_{\text{eff}}\;=\;s\cdot\mathbb{E}\big|\mathcal{A}\big|, (57) where s s is the loss scale of equation 22 . Since the regression target departs from the anchor by exactly 𝒜 ​ δ \mathcal{A}\,\delta , the quantity η eff \eta_{\text{eff}} measures, up to the residual norm, how far each update asks the policy to move; it is the natural common currency for comparing an exponential and a linear tilt, whose advantages have different scales by construction. The second is ‖ 𝒇 θ − 𝒇 old ‖ 2 \|{\bm{f}}_{\theta}-{\bm{f}}_{\mathrm{old}}\|^{2} . Here 𝒇 old {\bm{f}}_{\mathrm{old}} is the exponential moving average of the policy, refreshed once per epoch and maintained in every configuration, so this is the policy–EMA gap: a proxy for how much the policy is currently changing. When the anchor is frozen it is in particular not the distance to the anchor, which is reported separately as ‖ 𝒇 θ − 𝒇 ref ‖ 2 \|{\bm{f}}_{\theta}-{\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}}\|^{2} , the squared distance to the adapter-disabled pretrained field averaged over the batch and over the sampled t t with the weights the loss itself uses. We report that second quantity as an implicit KL because it is proportional to the per-step KL under the Gaussian transitions, and all read-outs of both are medians over an explicitly stated epoch window. The third is the fraction of prompt groups whose reward has zero variance, which measures how much of the batch still carries a usable learning signal as the reward saturates. Figure 6: Generalization to Pickscore reward. DiffusionRFT achieves consistent superiority over DiffusionNFT, as displayed by training reward (a) and validation reward (b).

sections.heading: Generalization experiments.
sections.text: To substantiate the generality and scalability of our method, we replicated the experiments on Pickscore, a learned preference model instead of a rule-based reward. As demonstrated in figure 6 , the results are consistent with the main paper. Our method delivers markedly faster convergence and reaches a higher performance ceiling than the competitor.

sections.heading: Why this is a misdirection and not a short step.
sections.text: A large regression loss admits two understandings, and they call for opposite remedies. Either the network has not yet moved far enough, in which case the loss is an excess over the floor and more optimization removes it, or it has moved as far as the target allows and the loss is the floor itself, in which case more optimization changes nothing and the target has to be reformulated. Equation 58 exactly discriminates these two cases, the excess being what Δ \Delta can still absorb and the floor being what it cannot, so the two understandings are distinguished by whether the movement budget has been spent. Figure 2 illustrates that the budget has been spent. The 𝒗 {\bm{v}} -space run moves as far as the 𝒙 {\bm{x}} -space one, 0.190 0.190 against 0.177 0.177 in ‖ 𝒇 θ − 𝒇 ref ‖ 2 \|{\bm{f}}_{\theta}-{\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}}\|^{2} , and it is handed more signal to move with 𝔼 ​ | 𝒜 | = 0.538 \mathbb{E}|\mathcal{A}|=0.538 against 0.420 0.420 . Nonetheless, it ends with 8.9 × 8.9\times the residual and less reward, 0.442 0.442 against 0.693 0.693 . A run that has spent its budget and still sits high above its counterpart is not taking short steps. That said, 8.9 × 8.9\times is not itself a pure measure of how much worse the fit is, because by equation 59 the two runs do not share a floor. The floor is a product of two factors and both differ. The advantage factor is 𝔼 ​ [ 𝒜 2 ] 𝒗 / 𝔼 ​ [ 𝒜 2 ] 𝒙 \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^{2}]_{{\bm{v}}}/\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^{2}]_{{\bm{x}}} , and we do not log the second moment directly. Each run supplies L ≤ 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝒜 2 ] ≤ U L\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^{2}]\leq U with L = ( 𝔼 ​ | 𝒜 | ) 2 L=(\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{A}|)^{2} and U = max i ⁡ | 𝒜 i | ​ 𝔼 ​ | 𝒜 | U=\max_{i}|\mathcal{A}_{i}|\,\mathbb{E}|\mathcal{A}| , and a ratio of two bracketed quantities is bracketed only across sides, L 𝒗 / U 𝒙 ≤ 𝔼 ​ [ 𝒜 2 ] 𝒗 / 𝔼 ​ [ 𝒜 2 ] 𝒙 ≤ U 𝒗 / L 𝒙 L_{{\bm{v}}}/U_{{\bm{x}}}\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^{2}]_{{\bm{v}}}/\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{A}^{2}]_{{\bm{x}}}\leq U_{{\bm{v}}}/L_{{\bm{x}}} , which at epoch 39 39 gives [ 0.69 , 4.07 ] [0.69,4.07] . The kernel factor is the t − 2 t^{-2} of equation 60 , worth 2.08 2.08 over the retained timesteps, so the floor ratio is known only to lie in [ 1.45 , 8.47 ] [1.45,8.47] , and the measured 8.9 8.9 nearly falls inside it. The excess over the floor is therefore not identified, and these statistics facilitate a scale analysis rather than a decomposition. That is enough for the conclusion it was meant to support: a regression loss is not comparable across prediction spaces, since here the change of floor alone can account for the entire measured ratio. One of the two floor factors deserves a comment. The advantage factor is larger for the 𝒗 {\bm{v}} -space run, but that is downstream of the failure rather than upstream. sections.heading: H.2 Why the dense linear tilt collapses.
sections.text: The instability of the unregularized linear tilt is not, however, a property of the linear family as such, and § 3.3 tells us where to look. Criterion equation 20 states that the centered form equation 19 is the χ 2 \chi^{2} optimum only while every relative tilt stays positive, equivalently min i ⁡ 𝒜 > − b \min_{i}\mathcal{A}>-b . At the b = 1 b=1 case used here the quantity to monitor is simply the smallest advantage in the batch. Doing so is decisive: the centered linear tilt spends 86.8 % 86.8\% of its training steps outside that regime and reaches min i ⁡ 𝒜 = − 2.46 \min_{i}\mathcal{A}=-2.46 , whereas over 928 928 steps of exponential-tilt training the bound 𝒜 ≥ − 1 \mathcal{A}\geq-1 is never approached, as the barrier property of f KL f_{\text{KL}} requires. Among the three runs the terminal drop is monotone in the effective step size equation 57 , η eff = 0.71 \eta_{\text{eff}}=0.71 , 0.90 0.90 and 2.11 2.11 giving drops of 0.001 0.001 , 0.046 0.046 and 0.185 0.185 . We posit that the collapse is the signature of a violated density constraint, and equation 21 supplies the corresponding repair: retain the projection in place of the dense approximation. We therefore probe the projection-only variant where the sparsemax advantage replaces the centered one, holding the constant baseline fixed so that the projection is the only variable that changes. Retaining the projection restores stability on its own: the sparsemax tilt ends 0.001 0.001 below its peak against 0.185 0.185 for the dense linear tilt.

sections.heading: H.3 How the optimal baseline comes into play.
sections.text: Two remarks are important regarding the constant b b in equation 12 , which the projection leaves free and which equation 23 then fixes by minimizing variance. First, b = 1 b=1 is the centering choice for every tilt considered here, and not a convention that happens to suit one of them: the relative tilt κ \kappa has group mean exactly one for the exponential weight of equation 13 , for the sparsemax weight of equation 21 by the construction of τ \tau , and for the dense linear weight, whose advantage ( R − R ¯ ) / γ (R-\bar{R})/\gamma in equation 19 is precisely κ − 1 \kappa-1 once κ = 1 + ( R − R ¯ ) / γ \kappa=1+(R-\bar{R})/\gamma is recognized. What varies between tilts is therefore not the centering constant but the spread of κ \kappa around it. Second, the baseline shift and the simplex projection of § 3.3 act on different objects and compose without interference: the projection enforces ρ ≥ 0 \rho\geq 0 and fixes the feasible set, while b ∗ b^{*} is a variance-reduction displacement applied afterwards, unbiased for any constant b b because 𝔼 ⁡ [ u t − v old ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[u_{t}-v^{\mathrm{old}}]=0 . Note finally that b ∗ b^{*} is estimated on the same micro-batch that it reweights, so the self-normalised control variate involves an 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / B ) \mathcal{O}(1/B) finite-batch bias. With the small micro-batches used here this term is not negligible, and the empirically observed sign of b ∗ b^{*} corresponds to a slight systematic pull of the regression target toward the sampled data.

sections.heading: What the control variate does.
sections.text: The grid above is unambiguous on the effect: without a control variate the dense linear tilt ends at 0.718 0.718 , with one it ends at 0.965 0.965 . Since variance reduction of order 10 − 4 10^{-4} cannot account for that, the stabilization must come from some other property of b ∗ b^{*} , and there are two candidates. It is a random variable, re-estimated on every micro-batch, so it has both a typical size and a tail; either could be doing the work. We separated them with four variants of the dense linear cell, each a single-key change. Two of the four keep the typical size and remove the tail: one replaces b ∗ b^{*} by the constant equal to its logged median, − 1.5 × 10 − 3 -1.5\times 10^{-3} , and the other clips | b ∗ | |b^{*}| at a running 90 90 th percentile. One keeps only the tail, zeroing b ∗ b^{*} below that quantile. The fourth caps | b ∗ | |b^{*}| at 1 % 1\% of the batch advantage magnitude. At a matched 390 390 epochs their terminal evaluation rewards are 0.941 0.941 , 0.111 0.111 , 0.847 0.847 and 0.000 0.000 , against 0.718 0.718 with no control variate and 0.964 0.964 with the optimal one. sections.heading: H.4 What confounds anchor-lock with RAM’s escape.
sections.text: The lock is not a property of the frozen anchor alone, and separating what it depends on also explains why RAM itself does not appear to suffer from the lock. Two quantities are confounded in a faithful RAM configuration. The first is how far the target is permitted to move off the anchor. RAM multiplies its advantage by 100 100 before adding it to the frozen base velocity. At unit multiplier the correction is roughly 40 × 40\times too weak to displace 𝒇 θ {\bm{f}}_{\theta} from 𝒇 ref {\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}} at all, which is exactly the regime the three stagnated variants sit in, and exactly the η eff \eta_{\text{eff}} of equation 57 being too small for the displacement the anchor demands. The second is where the anchor sits. RAM trains with classifier-free guidance at scale 2.0 2.0 , whereas our grid is CFG-free throughout. The base model’s own training reward is 0.164 0.164 without guidance against 0.410 0.410 with it, so the two setups anchor to pretrained behaviors of very different quality. Zhu et al. (2026) identify precisely the second effect, observing that anchoring to the weaker non-CFG conditional model can dominate the reward term and pull the policy towards low-quality regions, and propose keeping the sampler CFG-free while anchoring the regularizer to the CFG-guided model. RAM does not make that separation: it simply guides both, but still enjoys the benefit. Raising the multiplier does lift the ceiling. Our faithful port reaches 0.711 0.711 from its higher starting point, and the official implementation reaches 1.000 1.000 in training reward. However, neither survives. Both collapse to zero afterwards, and the diagnostics of figure 3 offer an explanation. With the anchor fixed, the displacement the target demands of a single update grows as the policy improves, while γ \gamma contracts towards its floor as the reward saturates, so the same multiplier that was barely sufficient early turns to be far too large late. In the sequel, we shed further light on the lock phenomenon of frozen anchors. We concentrate on the signal first. Frozen anchors give 𝔼 ​ | 𝒜 | = 0.49 \mathbb{E}|\mathcal{A}|=0.49 to 0.58 0.58 against 0.29 0.29 for the rolling anchor, and their reward has not saturated. The zero-variance group fraction stays at 0.000 0.000 and the within-group reward standard deviation at 0.40 0.40 , whereas under the rolling anchor the first rises from 0 0 to 0.479 0.479 and the second falls from 0.485 0.485 to 0.094 0.094 . The configuration that wins is the one running out of signal, and the configuration that keeps its signal is the one that stalls. Two further quantities separate local change from net displacement. The first is the distance to 𝒇 old {\bm{f}}_{\mathrm{old}} . The frozen speed stays within 2.6 2.6 to 3.7 × 10 − 6 3.7\times 10^{-6} in all three runs, while the rolling speed crosses that ceiling at epoch 8 8 and ends four orders of magnitude above it. The second is the distance to 𝒇 ref {\bm{f}}_{\text{ref}} , which is the quantity we report as an implicit KL and to which it is proportional under the Gaussian transitions. It separates the two configurations with no crossover at all, 1.9 1.9 to 4.5 × 10 − 4 4.5\times 10^{-4} for the frozen runs against 1.5 × 10 − 1 1.5\times 10^{-1} , and split by fifths of the window it grows 4.4 × 4.4\times under the rolling anchor and not at all under a frozen one, ending at 0.3 0.3 to 0.8 0.8 of where it started. The frozen policy is held in a neighborhood, it is not drifting slowly out of one. Terminal training rewards for the three frozen variants are 0.249 0.249 , 0.246 0.246 and 0.248 0.248 , against 0.980 0.980 for the rolling-anchor run. For the two RAM implementations, comparing medians over the 80 80 epochs before the evaluation peak with the 120 120 after it, we find that the official run moves from 0.98 0.98 to 0.92 0.92 in reward and from 0.23 0.23 to 0.36 0.36 in advantage magnitude, while its output-delta norm, a norm rather than the squared distance above, grows 7.2 × 7.2\times ( 0.031 → 0.224 0.031\to 0.224 ), its target norm from 836 836 to 1437 1437 , and its gradient norm 3.4 × 3.4\times ( 0.46 → 1.55 0.46\to 1.55 ). Our reproduction logs the gradient norm but not the displacement, and shows the same runaway in milder form, 1.3 × 1.3\times ( 0.57 → 0.76 0.57\to 0.76 ). The failure is therefore a runaway of the target rather than a loss of signal. The anchor is fixed while 𝒜 ​ δ \mathcal{A}\,\delta is scaled by 100 100 , the target separates from the field the sampler uses, and the regression amplifies its own error. A rolling anchor removes this feedback path, because the anchor follows the policy and the target cannot separate from the sampling distribution indefinitely.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.33444v1 [cs.LG] 27 Sep 2026 Elucidating the Design Space of Regression-based Diffusion Reinforcement Learning Toyota Li David Zhao & Alan Zhao Affiliation: Tencent Abstract A nascent family of methods that forgoes the policy gradient and reweights a supervised regression instead has garnered momentum in reinforcement learning for diffusion and flow models. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) , FlowAWR ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , and RAM ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) are representative regimes with contrasting motivations. It is yet opaque what, if anything, they share. We substantiate that each is the solution of one divergence-constrained reward-maximization problem, and they are differentiated only by the convex generator that defines the constraint. Under the unified modeling framework, we unravel the relaxations that prior art made during building the advantage-embedded regression target: approximating the KKT condition and posterior normalizer for the linear and exponential tilt shapes DiffusionNFT and FlowAWR respectively, while preserving the exact sparsemax projection onto the probability simplex for linear tilt leads to another superior model type in this work. Beyond the theoretical underpinnings, we further empirically investigate the design space and shed light on the training recipe for regression-style diffusion RL. Retaining the merits discovered during our exploration gives rise to DiffusionRFT, our paradigm that converges faster, trains more stably, and attains the top performance. 1 Introduction Post-training with an external reward plays a pivotal role in endowing a diffusion model with human-preference behaviors that pre-training dictates only weakly, such as prompt adherence and text rendering. Reinforcement learning serves as a cornerstone of this utility. The trailblazers in this field are the policy gradient ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ) and direct reward backpropagation ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2024 ; Prabhudesai et al., 2024 ) scheme. Nevertheless, they are both cumbersome, in that a long denoising trajectory is indispensable and exhibits high variance. Moreover, the training objective diverges from the simple Mean-Squared Error (MSE) loss prevalent in pre-training, that is believed to simplify the generative distribution modeling to supervised learning, especially at scale. Recently, a growing body of forward-process policy optimization ushers in a new wave of diffusion RL, including DiffusionNFT, FlowAWR and RAM, which reserve the regular diffusion loss and inject a reward into the regression target, so that a policy update is again a least-square fit on noised samples. These algorithms are grounded in divergent perspectives, ranging from CFG-style contrastive rectification Chen et al. (2025) to stochastic optimal control ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) . Worse still, they are separately presented as standalone and integrated systems. The missing piece is a principled account of their subtle interweaving, and which design decisions drive the performance. To bridge this gap, we uncover that one optimization step underlying these RL algorithms converges to a common driving force: maximize reward on a frozen rollout buffer under a divergence penalty. The divergence penalty translates the primary algorithmic choice into a single convex generator f f (equation 2 ). The reverse-KL generator yields the exponential tilt, whose group estimator coincides with the FlowAWR objective, while the Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} generator yields a linear tilt, that DiffusionNFT already applies by standardizing the reward within a prompt group and dividing by a heuristic constant, but without such a derivation. As stated above, permitting the realization of the unified optimization objective demands an additional approximation, estimating a posterior normalizer by its endpoint counterpart. We demonstrate it preserves the direction of every step exactly while rescaling its length by a factor with unit mean and variance bounded by the second moment of the advantage. The Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} case turns out to be the more promising one, to which most of our research endeavor is devoted. Its exact constrained optimum is a Euclidean projection onto the probability simplex, that is the sparsemax weight, whereas the linear advantage heuristically adopted by DiffusionNFT keeps only the interior branch of the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions and silently drops the constraint that relative densities stay non-negative. We articulate the condition under which the dense form is exact, observe that it is violated by the dense linear tilt on most training steps, and the training collapses afterwards. Retaining the projection repairs the collapse and achieves higher rewards. We term our resulting method Diffusion Regression Fine-tuning , or DiffusionRFT, a notably more stable and efficient point in this design space. Beyond the scope of our derivation lie the empirical design choices. The remainder is cast into four axes: the regression variable, the reward shaping and its baseline, the anchor from which the target is displaced, and the law governing the renoising timestep, and we adjust each in isolation. The regression variable lays the groundwork for subsequent algorithmic axes. Empirical results advocate the sparsemax tilt in line with our exact derivation. Meanwhile, an analytically variance-minimizing baseline further facilitates performance stabilization and enhancement across all tilts. A frozen anchor, though supported by RAM, admits no safe operating point, regardless of the update magnitude. Decoupling the renoising timestep from the generating trajectory, which might be assumed to enrich the experience buffer, instead steers the loss toward noise levels the sampler never visits. 2 Reward Maximization under a Divergence Constraint 2.1 Policy Improvement on a Frozen Rollout Buffer The policy-gradient family, from pioneering PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) to the critic-free estimators of GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , alternates between drawing trajectories from a behavior policy π old \pi^{\mathrm{old}} and updating the current policy π θ \pi_{	heta} on the resulting batch.
